summary: Describes a method for encapsulating AX.25 frames, the amateur packet-radio link-layer protocol, within IP packets. It is an Experimental protocol.

eli5.summary: Ham radio operators have their own message format. This lets them ride inside Internet packets.

questions: how to encapsulate ax.25 in ip
how to send ax.25 over internet
subtitle: Carries amateur radio packet protocol inside Internet packets

tldr.problem: Amateur radio operators using AX.25 (the packet-radio link-layer protocol) need a way to carry those frames over the Internet Protocol.
tldr.mechanism: Each AX.25 frame is placed directly inside an IP datagram with protocol number 93, omitting HDLC framing but preserving the frame check sequence.
tldr.outcome: Amateur radio networks can interconnect over the Internet while preserving AX.25 message integrity.

today: RFC 1226 is an Experimental protocol document that defines the encapsulation method. Amateur radio networks continue to use AX.25 frames, though modern deployments also use newer protocols.

sections.title: Amateur Radio over IP
sections.content: The AX.25 Amateur Packet-Radio Link-Layer Protocol defines how amateur (ham) radio operators exchange messages via packet radio. To allow AX.25 frames to travel across the Internet, they must be encapsulated in IP datagrams. Each AX.25 frame becomes the payload of one IP packet, assigned IP protocol number 93.
sections.eli5: Ham radio messages need to be packed into Internet packets, so they can travel across the Internet and still be recognized when they arrive.

sections.title: Frame Encapsulation
sections.content: When an AX.25 frame is encapsulated in IP, the HDLC framing elements (flags and zero-stuffing) are removed because the IP datagram already marks the frame boundaries. The 16-bit CRC-CCITT frame check sequence is preserved intact. AX.25 frames normally do not exceed 330 octets, so IP fragmentation is typically not necessary, though larger frames can use standard IP fragmentation if needed.
sections.eli5: The ham radio message part is copied directly into the Internet packet, but some of the radio packaging is removed because the Internet packet provides its own wrapping.

sections.title: Protocol Numbers and Standards
sections.content: Each IP datagram carrying an AX.25 frame uses protocol number 93. The document references the AX.25 Amateur Packet-Radio Link-Layer Protocol Version 2.0 from October 1984, available from the American Radio Relay League. The RFC specifies only the basic encapsulation; security considerations for amateur radio networks over IP are not addressed in this document.
sections.eli5: The Internet uses protocol number 93 to mean "this packet carries an AX.25 radio message". The details of AX.25 itself come from the ham radio standard.

references.text: AX.25 Amateur Packet-Radio Link-Layer Protocol Version 2.0, October 1984. American Radio Relay League, Newington CT USA 06111.
